messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 55-year-old fashion designer who came to treatment after years of insisting he had simply become “difficult” with age. He grew up in a house where danger arrived through the person meant to protect him. His caregiver’s physical abuse was unpredictable, often happening in stretches of unnatural quiet that made him listen for footsteps, a shift in breathing, the touch of a hand on his shoulder that could turn, without warning, into violence. What remained with him was not a single clean account but broken sensory fragments and a bodily certainty that silence meant something bad was about to happen. Even now he cannot tell a clear story of what happened from beginning to end. At times he can describe an incident in a flat, detached way, as if he were talking about someone else’s childhood, and then without warning a shard of memory brings a surge of guilt so strong that he feels implicated in his own suffering.

As an adult, David built a life around beauty, control, and presentation. In his studio, where assistants move around him pinning fabric and adjusting garments on models, he has become known for flinching sharply if someone touches him from behind. He covers it with irritability or precision, but inside the reaction feels immediate and absolute. He has come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that something in him was permanently altered by what happened. The fact that he still startles, still scans even his own apartment at night, has convinced him at times that he may be going crazy. Those beliefs do not sit quietly in the background; they shape how he moves through the world, leaving him on guard at home and especially unsettled by silence, which feels less peaceful than ominous, as though it is the moment before something terrible begins again.

The memories and the meaning he makes of them feed each other. Because the abuse comes back in disconnected pieces, David takes the gaps as evidence of damage: if he cannot form a coherent story, he thinks, then his mind must be broken. When he recalls the past in an emotionless, almost foreign way, that numbness frightens him as much as the content itself; it seems to confirm his fear that he has been changed for the worse. And when guilt arrives during recall, he turns it inward and outward at once, dwelling on what he must have done wrong while also circling for hours around what other people did to him and how unprotected he was. The more he remembers in fragments, the more mistrustful and self-condemning he becomes.

Over time David developed rituals to manage this. He avoids times of day and situations that he associates with nightmares, delaying sleep with work, television, or pacing around the apartment rather than lying in the dark when the quiet closes in. He ruminates constantly—sometimes accusing himself, sometimes replaying the injuries done by others—because he feels that if he could only think hard enough, he might finally make sense of it or assign blame correctly. These habits are driven by his beliefs that people are dangerous, that he has been permanently damaged, and that his reactions signal mental collapse. Yet the effect is the opposite of relief. By refusing the times that bring dreams and by spending hours trapped in repetitive blame, he never arrives at a fuller narrative; the memory remains jagged, numb in places and contaminated by guilt in others. Each failed attempt to think his way through it leaves him more convinced that something is fundamentally wrong with him.

His state of alarm also pulls the past closer. On nights when his apartment falls silent, he checks locks, listens for sounds in the hallway, and feels watchful even in bed. After an unexpected touch at work—a seamstress brushing his arm to get his attention, a model stepping too close backstage—he can spend the rest of the day with old fragments pressing in, not as a complete recollection but as bodily knowledge and flashes he cannot organize. That renewed contact with memory deepens his conviction that he is unsafe and unstable. In turn, those convictions heighten his vigilance, making silence more menacing and ordinary contact more startling.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had begun to cost him professionally and personally. Assistants had started avoiding him because his sharp reactions to touch felt hostile, and his adult daughter had told him that being in his apartment was exhausting because he was always listening, always tense. What finally brought him in was a recent night when he sat awake until dawn to avoid dreaming and found himself thinking, with unusual clarity, that he could not keep living as if the danger were still in the room. He is most afraid that the damage is permanent and that his mind is slipping beyond his control, but he is also hoping, cautiously, that if he can understand what happens to him when the silence comes, the past may stop ruling every room he enters.
